title: Joan of Arc (1412–1431)
hookLine: a farm girl who led armies, was burned at nineteen, and was declared innocent 25 years later

cards: France, 1429, deep in a war with England that has dragged on for generations. A peasant girl of about seventeen, from a village in the east, who can't read or write, walks into the court of the uncrowned king.
God has sent her, she tells him, to lift the siege of Orléans and see him crowned. Nobody expects her, and plenty doubt her. She has no title and no training.
Within a few months, the siege is lifted and the king is crowned.

teach.b: Joan said that from about the age of thirteen she heard voices, which she identified as Saint Michael, Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret. They told her to go and help the king.

She cut her hair, put on armor, and rode at the front of the army carrying a banner. At her trial she said she loved her banner far more than her sword, and carried it so she wouldn't have to kill anyone.

That summer the king was crowned at Reims, with Joan beside him. Then it fell apart. A year later she was captured and sold to the English, who tried her before a church court run by a bishop on their side.
She had no lawyer. For months, learned men tried to trap her.
One trap became well-known: are you in God's grace? Say yes, and she's proud.
Say no, and she's condemned herself.

teach.h: IF I AM NOT, MAY GOD PUT ME THERE.
teach.b: A nineteen-year-old with no schooling answered, in effect: if I am not, may God put me there, and if I am, may God keep me there. By later accounts, her questioners were stunned. They burned her anyway, in Rouen, in 1431.

She asked for a cross to be held up where she could see it. Twenty-five years later, with the pope's approval, a new church trial declared the first one unjust and cleared her name. In 1920 she was declared a saint.

So the same Church that condemned her, through a bishop, later admitted it was wrong and honored her. Today's line, I am not afraid, is a saying people hang on her; that exact sentence isn't in the trial records.
What the records do hold is a teenager answering learned men for months without backing down.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Joan of Arc on 30 May; she is one of the patron saints of France, and many ask her prayers for courage.

games.q: you're Joan, nineteen, on trial. a judge asks: are you in God's grace? yes sounds proud. no condemns you. what do you say?
o: if I am not, may God put me there; if I am, may God keep me there.

practice: Think of one place where you know what's right but have stayed quiet, at work, in your family, among friends, and notice whether fear sits somewhere in your body. Don't push it away; Joan wept at her trial, and kept answering.
Picture one small step you could take, and if you pray, ask for her courage.
